children.text: Saints Peter and Paul Parish Church in the middle of Bantayan Town traces back to a parish first founded by Augustinian friars in 1580. The present stone church was completed in 1863, and it is known for its ceiling mural painted in 2018–2019 and for its Holy Week procession.

Saints Peter and Paul Parish Church is a Roman Catholic parish church in Bantayan Town, the center of Bantayan Island. Its official parish name is the Parish of Saint Peter Apostle (Parroquia de San Pedro Apostol). In the 1980s a parish priest added Saint Paul as a second patron, and the name "Saints Peter and Paul" became widely used. In 2022 Bishop Emilio Bataclan of the Archdiocese of Cebu reaffirmed the original name and adopted a parish logo. So even if names differ on map apps or in guides, it is the same church.

The parish began in 1580. Wikipedia says Augustinian priests built the first church on June 15, 1580, while other media and guides give June 11, so the dates differ. Either way it dates to June 1580, and it is described as the oldest parish outside Manila and the first parish founded in the Visayas and Mindanao. The parish existed before the Diocese of Cebu was created in 1595, and records say its jurisdiction once reached Maripipi (in present-day Biliran) and Limangcawayan in Leyte. It was first known as the Convento de la Asuncion de Nuestra Senora.

The church has been rebuilt several times. After Muslim raiders burned it in 1600 it was rebuilt soon after, and the present building is a Baroque coral-stone church begun in 1839 and finished in 1863. It has a high ceiling, a rectangular plan and a gabled roof, and although it has been repaired many times, much of the coral-stone foundation and walls are said to remain.

The church matters to travelers for two reasons. One is the ceiling mural begun in September 2018 and finished in 2019, and the other is the large Holy Week procession of sacred images held every year. Outside service times you can look around quietly, and it fits well into a half-day plan with the plaza, the market and the Obo-ob mangrove park in Bantayan Town. However, the church was partly damaged in the September 30, 2025 northern Cebu earthquake, so check locally whether you can go in before you visit.

The ceiling of the church carries a mural of about 1,130 m². Wikipedia says it was begun in September 2018 and completed in 2018–2019 by twelve artists from Cebu and Leyte under Aris Avelino Pastor. A SunStar article lists six artists and says parish priest Joselito Danao commissioned it as a "visual catechism," so the number and names of the artists differ between sources. The themes are Creation, the Fall of Man and Redemption, and above the altar are brightly colored scenes of the Coronation of the Virgin and the Resurrection.

According to a SunStar article of November 2018, the ceiling was bare until August 2018 and the artists painted by hand every day from September. By mid-November the section above the altar was finished, and the plan was to complete the whole ceiling by Holy Week 2019. The work was demanding because of the height and heat, and the team included an eighteen-year-old apprentice from Bantayan. The cost was estimated at a minimum of
, raised through donations from residents, Bantayanons abroad and benefactors, with the blessing of the Commission on Culture and Heritage of the Archdiocese of Cebu.

The facade and walls are built of coral stone in the Baroque style, and one guide mentions stone reliefs of saints. Coral stone was a common material on islands near the sea, and you can see a rough texture that has stood for a long time. Check on site how repairs of the earthquake-damaged parts are going and follow the safety signs.

blocks.title: History of the parish and church

children.text: The church was where Spanish missionaries first established a parish on this island, and it is described as giving Bantayanons an early start in education. Wikipedia says that on July 27, 1824 Pope Leo XII granted the islanders an indult exempting them from Lenten meat abstinence, valid until 1843. Some reports date the same privilege to the 1840s or the 1880s, so the media disagree.

blocks.title: The Holy Week Santo Entierro procession

children.text: The procession that leaves the church on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday is the biggest sight. Carriages (carrozas) bearing life-size figures show scenes of the Passion of Christ as they go through the streets. One report says Bantayan has 34 Holy Week carriages, the biggest in Cebu, while another says the figures are mostly made by local sculptors and mixed with old images brought from Spain more than a century ago. It is also said that old families compete to build the most impressive carriage.

blocks.title: The Holy Week meat and fishing custom

children.text: While other places avoid meat in Holy Week, Bantayan is described as serving lechon and other meat and seafood, and instead resting from fishing. Wikipedia explains that the fishermen's rest from fishing during the church's rebuilding led to the present custom, but this is an interpretation, so follow local explanations first. The market stays busy until Good Friday.

blocks.title: Feast of Saints Peter and Paul

children.text: The feast day honoring the church's patron saints is June 29. The Palawod festival held that day in Bantayan Town is the town's biggest event, combining a parade honoring fishing with street events. The date and program change from year to year, so check municipal or parish announcements.

Most lodging is concentrated near the beaches of Santa Fe, and Bantayan Town has small guesthouses and restaurants. In Holy Week thousands arrive and resorts fill up, and people without a room sometimes sleep on the beach in tents or on mats, while backpackers are said to sleep in the town plaza. If you go then, book several months ahead.

At the market near the church you can eat fish dishes and local snacks cheaply, and in Holy Week the market stays busy until Good Friday. For the market and the Obo-ob mangrove eco park, see the Bantayan Town entry.
A church is a place of prayer, so be quiet during Mass and dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered.
Visiting may be difficult during Mass or events, so check the times with the parish or the local notice board before you go.
The ceiling mural is best seen by looking up, so early hours when sunlight comes in are good. Follow local guidance on whether photography is allowed.
Ferry tickets sell out early in Holy Week. It is safer to plan to arrive before Maundy Thursday.
During the procession the streets narrow around the carriages, so keep your belongings secure and hold children by the hand.
The sun around the church is strong. Bring a hat and water.
Check local announcements on the earthquake recovery and do not trust old information.

Knowing the history, such as the 1600 raid and rebuilding and the 1839–1863 construction, will make the stone walls around the plaza look different. You can ask a priest or the parish office for an explanation on site.
The church is known to have been partly damaged by the September 30, 2025 northern Cebu earthquake. There may be entry restrictions or repair work, so always confirm locally whether it is open.
The founding date, the year of the indult and the number of artists differ between sources. Give priority to the explanations on site.
Holy Week ferry fares and times change a lot and tickets sell out easily.
Crowds gather during the procession. Watch out for pickpockets and congestion.
It is a place of faith, so avoid shorts or sleeveless tops, loud noise and flash photography.
In the June–November rainy season and typhoon months, ferries may be canceled.
